item.title: 49-50: Four Republicans Break Ranks in the Senate's Last Iran War Vote Before the Midterms
item.body:
The U.S. Senate came within one vote on Thursday of directing President Donald Trump to end American military action against Iran. The resolution failed 49-50, even though four Republicans sided with Democrats to support it. With no further votes expected before the November elections, the war now moves from the Senate floor to the campaign trail.

## What Happened

On September 24, 2026, the Senate voted on H.Con.Res. 89, a war powers resolution the House had passed in July by a vote of 214-208. The measure would have directed the president to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities against Iran unless Congress explicitly authorized the conflict through a declaration of war or a specific authorization for the use of military force.

The final tally was 49 in favor and 50 opposed. Most Republicans voted no. The resolution drew support from nearly every Democrat and from four Republicans:

- **Susan Collins** of Maine
- **Lisa Murkowski** of Alaska
- **Rand Paul** of Kentucky
- **Thom Tillis** of North Carolina

Two Democratic senators did not vote with their party. Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania voted no, and Sen. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland did not vote. Reports noted that supporters would have needed full Democratic attendance and a fifth Republican to prevail.

## Why Tillis's Vote Matters

Paul, Collins and Murkowski have backed similar measures before. Tillis, who is leaving the Senate at the end of his term, joined them in supporting the measure this time. He said his reasoning was tied to the clock in the 1973 War Powers Resolution. That law requires the president to notify Congress when forces are committed to hostilities. It also limits unauthorized engagement to 60 days, with a possible 30-day extension for withdrawal. Tillis pointed out that more than 60 days had passed since the administration notified Congress in July that military action had resumed.

He also said the administration needs to keep Congress better informed about its strategic objectives. In his words, "They need to inform Congress more."

## A Long Series of Votes

This was far from the first attempt. Democrats have forced more than a dozen votes on Iran war powers since the U.S. began military operations in late February, and news outlets have counted the latest vote as the 12th or 14th in the series. The results have varied. An earlier measure advanced with four Republican supporters, and a June resolution cleared the Senate narrowly. That support did not last, and the White House dismissed the June measure as poorly timed and meaningless.

Because the measure was a concurrent resolution, it would not have required the president's signature. Even so, the executive branch has shown no sign that it would change course based on a symbolic vote.

Sen. Tim Kaine, a Virginia Democrat who has led the push for these votes, said Republicans "have been carrying water for this ridiculous and illegal war for months." Republican leaders have described the situation differently. Senate Majority Leader John Thune acknowledged what he called "voter fatigue" over high fuel prices and said he hoped the administration is focused on reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

## The Cost Beyond the Capitol

The political pressure comes largely from the economy. Iran has turned the Strait of Hormuz, a key shipping lane for the world's oil, into a war zone in response to U.S. strikes. Prices for gasoline, diesel, fertilizer and food have risen as a result. Reports cited during the coverage of the vote put the war's cost to date at about $43.5 billion, with diesel above $6 per gallon in some areas and the national average for gasoline near $4.48. Those figures come from individual news reports and vary by source and date.

Public opinion is a second source of pressure. An NBC News poll found 62% of voters saying the war has not been worth it, against 33% who said it has. By a 57%-24% margin, voters said they would prefer a candidate who opposes the conflict.

## The Republican Balancing Act

The vote also showed how Republicans in competitive races are handling the issue. Several GOP candidates have recently sharpened their criticism of the war's effect on household costs. Yet most Republican senators facing tough races still voted against the resolution. That split, criticizing the consequences of the war while declining to constrain the president, is likely to draw scrutiny from both parties in the coming weeks.

Supporters of the administration's approach argue that the U.S. needs to re-establish deterrence after American service members were killed and wounded. Sen. Dan Sullivan of Alaska made a version of that case, arguing that a country whose troops have suffered such losses needs to restore deterrence. Opponents counter that a war of this scale requires explicit congressional approval and a clear plan for how it ends.

## What Comes Next

With the Senate expected to leave for the campaign season, this was likely the last floor vote on the war before Election Day. Congress can still shape the conflict through funding. Reports say a White House request for roughly $87.6 billion in additional war funding remains stalled. Whichever party controls each chamber next year will have considerable influence over that request.

For voters, the message from the vote is that the debate over the Iran war has not ended in Washington. It has moved to the ballot box. The 49-50 result suggests that a small change in the Senate's makeup could decide future war powers votes. The war's costs at home, and the future of U.S. involvement abroad, are likely to weigh on many voters' decisions this fall.

## Sources and Notes

This article is a summary based on reporting from CBS News, NPR, NBC News, ABC News, CNBC and MS NOW, along with the Senate Press Gallery's record of the vote. Figures on costs, prices and casualties vary between outlets and change over time. Readers should check the latest reporting for updated numbers. This article is for general information only. It does not endorse any candidate, party or policy position.
